lessons.title: IT Services: Deal Wins, Attrition, Utilisation, and the Rupee-Dollar Link

body.text: Indian IT services companies earn in dollars, euros, and pounds, and spend mostly in rupees on people. Almost everything that matters in the sector follows from that: growth depends on how much global clients spend on technology, margins depend on how efficiently engineers are deployed and what they are paid, and the exchange rate quietly adds or subtracts profit every quarter.

children.text: IT is the second largest sector in the Nifty 50, and companies like TCS, Infosys, HCLTech, Wipro, and Tech Mahindra are among the most widely held stocks in Indian portfolios and mutual funds. Yet many investors track them only by the headline profit number. This lesson teaches you to read an IT company the way the sector's analysts do, through a handful of operating metrics that explain the headline before it changes.
The Business Model: Selling Skilled Hours to Global Clients

Indian IT firms build, run, and modernise technology systems for large companies, mostly in North America and Europe. Banking and financial services clients are typically the largest vertical, followed by retail, manufacturing, communications, and healthcare. Work is delivered mainly from offshore centres in cities like Bengaluru, Pune, Chennai, and Hyderabad, with a smaller team onsite at client locations. Contracts are priced as time and materials (billing for hours worked), fixed price (a set fee for a defined outcome), or long-term managed services.

columns.label: Run-the-business spending
points: Maintaining existing systems, infrastructure management, application support
Sticky and relatively resilient in a slowdown
Clients push for cost cuts and vendor consolidation, which pressures pricing

columns.label: Discretionary spending
points: New digital projects, cloud migrations, consulting, and transformation work
Shorter projects that can be paused quickly
Surges in booms, as in 2021 and early 2022
The first thing clients cut when their own business slows

children.text: Growth: Always Start With Constant Currency

markDefs.definition: Revenue growth calculated as if exchange rates had not changed from the comparison period. It isolates real business growth from currency movements.

children.text: An IT company's revenue growth can be reported in three ways, and they can tell three different stories. Rupee growth includes the effect of the rupee against all currencies. Dollar growth includes the effect of the euro and pound against the dollar, called cross-currency movement.

strips out all currency effects and shows how much more work the company actually did for clients. It is the number management and analysts anchor on, and the basis for revenue guidance where companies such as Infosys provide it.

body.title: The Rupee-Powered Headline
body.scenario: An IT company's results headline reads: 'Revenue up 9% year on year in rupee terms, a strong quarter.' In the fact sheet, revenue grew 4% in US dollar terms and 2% in constant currency terms. During the year the rupee weakened meaningfully against the dollar, and the euro strengthened against the dollar.
body.prompt: How strong was the quarter really? Explain the gap between the three growth numbers.
body.modelAnswer: The underlying business grew only 2%, which is the constant currency figure and the real measure of demand. The gap between 2% constant currency and 4% dollar growth came from cross-currency movement: revenue billed in euros converted into more dollars because the euro strengthened. The further gap between 4% dollar growth and 9% rupee growth came from the weaker rupee, which converted each dollar into more rupees. Neither currency effect reflects more work won from clients, and both can reverse. It was a weak quarter for demand dressed up by currency tailwinds. Watch whether constant currency growth improves in coming quarters, and whether margins benefited from the rupee in a way that could fade.

children.text: Deal Wins: The Best Lead Indicator

Most large IT firms disclose the total contract value (TCV) of deals signed each quarter, and some separately report large deals above a threshold. TCV is spread over the life of a contract, so a $1.5 billion deal over five years adds about $300 million of revenue a year once fully ramped up, and often less in the first year. Watch the trend over four or more quarters, not one quarter, because a single mega deal can distort it. Also ask how much of the TCV is genuinely new business rather than renewals of existing contracts; management usually discloses this as 'net new' TCV.

body.title: Pick the Leading Indicator
body.question: You want the best signal of an IT company's revenue growth over the next four quarters. Which combination is most useful?
options: Last quarter's net profit growth and dividend per share
Trailing four-quarter deal TCV trend, the share of net new deals, and net headcount additions
Rupee revenue growth and the USD/INR rate
The P/E ratio compared with its five-year average
body.explanation: Signed deals convert into future revenue, and companies hire ahead of expected work, so a rising TCV trend with healthy net new deals and positive headcount additions points to growth ahead. Profit and dividends look backward, rupee growth is distorted by currency, and P/E is a valuation measure, not a demand signal.

children.text: Margins: People, Utilisation, and the Pyramid

Employee costs are by far the largest expense for an IT services company. So margins depend on how productively the workforce is used and how much it costs. Utilisation is the share of available employee time that is billed to clients; staff on the bench between projects and trainees are paid but not billed. The pyramid is the mix of experience levels: more freshers at the base and fewer senior staff lowers average cost per employee. Attrition, the rate at which employees leave, forces companies to replace people at higher salaries, pay retention bonuses, and use costlier subcontractors in the meantime.

body.title: Illustrative IT Company: Attrition vs EBIT Margin Over a Boom and Slowdown

children.text: This pattern mirrors what the Indian IT industry went through after the pandemic. During the 2021 to 2022 demand boom, companies hired aggressively, attrition at several large firms climbed above 20%, salary costs jumped, and margins fell even as revenue grew strongly. When client spending slowed from 2023, hiring was cut, attrition fell back, and margins recovered partly through lower attrition and better utilisation, even though revenue growth became sluggish. Revenue growth and margins often move in opposite directions in this sector.

stats.label: Extra revenue
stats.context: With almost no extra salary cost, since these people were already on the payroll

children.text: In Chapter 2 you saw that a weaker rupee lifts rupee revenue for exporters. For IT, the margin effect is what matters. Offshore salaries are paid in rupees, while onsite staff, travel, and some subcontractors are paid in dollars. When the rupee weakens, revenue in rupees rises in full, dollar costs rise in rupees too, but rupee costs do not change. The gap flows to margin. Companies hedge a portion of expected dollar revenue with forward contracts, which smooths both the gains and the losses.

body.title: Calculate the New EBIT Margin
body.prompt: Using the table above, what is the company's EBIT margin at a USD/INR rate of 84? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: EBIT at 84 = ₹8,400 crore - ₹2,520 crore - ₹3,600 crore = ₹2,280 crore. EBIT margin = 2,280 ÷ 8,400 = 27.1%. A 5% depreciation in the rupee added about 2.1 percentage points to margin without any change in the underlying business. In reality, hedging, wage hikes, and client pricing pressure usually absorb part of this benefit, so treat currency-driven margin gains as temporary.

body.text: Generative AI and automation are changing IT services economics. Clients increasingly expect productivity gains to be passed on as lower prices, which can shrink revenue for the same scope of work even as new AI projects create demand. Listen closely to management commentary on pricing in renewals, not just on new AI deal wins.

body.explanation: Utilisation measures how productively the paid workforce is deployed. Raising it lifts revenue with little extra cost, which directly improves margins.

body.title: Reading an IT Company's Quarterly Results
steps: Start with constant currency revenue growth, quarter on quarter and year on year, and compare it with any guidance
Note the gap between constant currency, dollar, and rupee growth to see how much currency flattered or hurt the headline
Check deal TCV for the quarter and the trailing four quarters, and the share of net new deals
Review growth by vertical and geography, especially banking and financial services and North America
Check EBIT margin and management's explanation of what moved it: currency, utilisation, wage hikes, or subcontracting
Track headcount additions, utilisation, and attrition as signals of demand and cost pressure
Compare all of the above with at least two peers, since sector-wide demand trends usually show up across companies

points: Indian IT firms earn mainly in foreign currencies and spend mainly in rupees on people, which shapes growth, margins, and currency sensitivity
Discretionary project spending surges in booms and is cut first in slowdowns; run-the-business spending is stickier
Constant currency growth is the true measure of demand; rupee and dollar growth can be flattered or hurt by currency
Deal TCV, especially net new deals, and headcount additions are the best lead indicators of future revenue
Margins depend on utilisation, the employee pyramid, attrition, subcontracting, and wage hikes
A weaker rupee lifts margins because rupee costs stay fixed, but hedging and pricing pressure absorb part of the gain
